newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks to retouch WW2 past with art exhibit.
newsitem.headline: France seeks to retouch WW2 past with art exhibit.

text.p: Seeking to lay to rest its troubled wartime past, France on Wednesday unveiled artworks recovered from Germany after World War Two in the hope that their owners would step forward and claim them.

"I want to prove that the reality is more complex than the rumours which say French museums conceal genuine 'treasures' seized from Jewish families by the Nazis," said Culture Minister Philippe Douste Blazy.
Next week, five state-run museums -- the Louvre, the Pompidou Centre, the Musee d'Orsay, Versailles and the Musee de Ceramique -- will show 900 unclaimed works of art entrusted to them after the war.

The decision came in the wake of a report by the powerful state spending watchdog, the Cour des Comptes, accusing state museums of failing in their legal duty to seek out the owners or heirs of some 2,000 works, including paintings by Picasso, Renoir, Monet, and Cezanne and sculptures by Rodin.

"If I have decided to have these works presented...it is because of a desire for openness," said Douste-Blazy, standing before a monumental oil painting by Gustave Courbet "The cliffs of Etretat after a storm", one of the most valuable works in the Musee d'Orsay exhibit.

While most of the works were sold to the Nazis by art dealers in the thriving wartime Paris art market, some are believed to have been seized from Jews deported to concentration camps, or sold under duress at rock-bottom prices.
Although it may never be known whether any of the 2,000 works were stolen from Jews, the issue is a moral one in a country whose collaborationist past was long taboo.
The exhibit also highlights the difficulty descendents of deported Jews have in proving a painting is rightfully theirs.

"My grandfather's house was completely looted during the war. I think one of the works in that room belonged to him, but how can I prove it? All the documents have been lost or destroyed," said one man, who declined to identify himself.
The show features such treasures as a Cezanne self-portrait, a "View of Argenteuil" by Monet or Alfred Sisley's "The Seine", as well as a series of drawings by Degas.

There is also an idealised 1891 portait of a statuesque girl and boy gazing at the sea by Alfred Stevens, which echoes Hitler's Aryan race propaganda and which he bought in 1942 for an undisclosed sum.
Most paintings have labels tracing the history of their owners to prove they were indeed sold, rather than seized from Jewish families.
But several others, such as a Renoir pastel "Head of a Young Girl", or a watercolour "Turkeys and a Duck" by Edouard Manet bear the words "Origin: Unknown."
At the end of the war, some 61,000 artworks were recovered from Germany, 45,441 of which were returned to their owners.

After the remaining works were displayed in the Chateau of Compiegne, north of Paris in the early 1950s, resulting in a handful of claims, the government sold off some 13,000 judged of little value. The remaining 2,000 were entrusted to the museums which were obliged under a 1949 law to try and locate the owners.
